Variants.Content: Enacted in 1258, the Provisions of Oxford came after Henry III's costly bid for the crown of Sicily left the treasury in debt and his government in disrepute. The baronial reformers forced the king to surrender much of his administrative power to a council of fifteen barons, led by Simon de Montfort. The Provisions also required Parliament to meet three times a year, so the Crown could be overseen in regular sessions rather than only when the king chose to summon his magnates. A standing council with the right to review royal decisions was unusual in English government. Its reach was limited, though, because the reformers formed a faction within the baronage and not a neutral body. Within a few years the dispute over the Provisions had turned into open civil war.

Simon de Montfort champions the reform of the realm under sworn communal oath, asserting that the Crown must govern by the counsel of its natural peers. Royalist lords denounce the Council of Fifteen as baronial tyranny usurping anointed royal prerogative.

White crosses are sewn onto the tunics of Montfortian knights who fortify the Tower of London. Common squires and burgesses have been summoned to council halls, and the power to bear arms in England no longer rests with the crown alone. Keep your place in the ranks and listen for the captain's orders.

Magnates quarrel over charters in Latin, while village bailiffs still levy heriot and tallage. A hungry serf knows little of councils; if the lords take their fight to the open fields, it is our thatched roofs that burn.
